The best plan is to wrap the code from the getActiveNetworkInfo call through the end of the switch in a try block, catching SecurityException. This safely handles the missing permission case.
remark: The call connectivityManager.getActiveNetworkInfo() may throw a SecurityException if the app lacks the ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE permission. The try-catch block wraps the code from getActiveNetworkInfo through the switch, and on catching SecurityException, returns C.NETWORK_TYPE_UNKNOWN to handle the exception gracefully.
analysis: The code flow: It first checks if context is null, returns UNKNOWN. Then gets ConnectivityManager via context.getSystemService, if null returns UNKNOWN. Then gets active network info via getActiveNetworkInfo(), if null or not connected returns OFFLINE. Then switches on network type to return appropriate constant. The call to connectivityManager.getActiveNetworkInfo() can throw a SecurityException (a runtime exception) if the app does not have the ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE permission. Additionally, the subsequent calls to networkInfo.isConnected(), networkInfo.getType(), and getMobileNetworkType() could theoretically throw runtime exceptions, but the most common and expected one is SecurityException from getActiveNetworkInfo(). Since the method does not catch any exceptions, and a SecurityException would propagate, it is advisable to catch it within this snippet to prevent the exception from bubbling up and to return a safe default value. The null checks already handle null objects, so no NullPointerException is expected from those. Only SecurityException is identified as a runtime exception that should be caught.
